newsitem.title: MALI: Opposition and security forces clash in Mali.
newsitem.headline: Opposition and security forces clash in Mali.

text.p: Opposition activists and security forces clashed in Mali's capital Bamako on Wednesday, when two opposition alliances tried to stage election protests in defiance of a government ban.

Witnesses said police used tear gas to disperse protesters in the city centre, where groups of opposition militants burned tyres and called for the government to resign and for elections to be suspended and reorganised after chaotic weekend polling.
Mali won widespread praise for its 1992 transition from single-party dictatorship to multi-party democracy.
Sunday's poll for a new 147-seat parliament and presidential and municipal elections in May and June are a test of how deeply democracy has taken root in the dirt-poor West African nation.
Early results released, point to a lead for President Alpha Oumar Konare's ruling ADEMA alliance, which won a 1992 poll, but with many seats needing to go to an April 27 second round.

The opposition alliances, who represent 11 parties and denounce the organisation of Sunday's poll as "shameful", want the results scrapped and say they will boycott the second round and the remaining elections.
They have called for the resignation of the Independent National Electoral Commission (CENI), which Konare set up under opposition pressure, saying it botched electoral arrangements.

Security forces on Wednesday barred protesters from the capital's Place de la Liberte square, focus of protests during the pro-democracy demonstrations that helped topple dictator Moussa Traore in 1991.

Some witnesses said 10 people were hurt elsewhere as security forces used truncheons or rubber bullets to stop large groups forming. Protesters walked around town chanting anti-government slogans and burned car tyres.
The government on Tuesday banned all street protests.
Sunday's vote launched Mali's second multi-party national polls since independence from France in 1960.
Voters turned out in force but many could not vote because of problems with voter cards, voter lists or ballot materials.

CENI president, lawyer Kassoum Tapo, blamed inadequate electoral lists. "The CENI is not an accomplice in any fraud, irregularity or sabotage of the elections," he told a Tuesday news conference. "We did absolutely everything we could so that our citizens could accomplish their civic duty," he said.
The two alliances, the opposition Front for Change and Democracy (FCD) and the Rally of Patriotic Forces (RFP) had denounced preparations for the elections before the poll.
The RFP includes supporters of the former single party and jailed former dictator Traore, whose overthrow cleared the way for democratic reform.
The FCD portrays itself as heir to the tradition of independence leader Modibo Keita, a nationalist and hardline socialist who declared a one-party state after independence.

Konare, a historian elected in 1992, had been due to face nine challengers in a May 4 presidential poll. He has steered Mali on a course of economic liberalisation, winning praise from the United States and the World Bank.
A total 1,500 candidates from 21 parties contested Sunday's election.
